name: Feynman's 1981 Idea
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Where the Whole Field Actually Started
lesson.summary: In a 1981 keynote, physicist Richard Feynman argued that classical computers can never efficiently simulate quantum mechanics and proposed building computers out of quantum systems instead, a narrower and more modest idea than the general-purpose quantum computer the public imagines today.
lesson.body:
Quantum computing is usually traced to a specific moment: a keynote talk Richard Feynman gave in May 1981 at a conference on the physics of computation, co-sponsored by MIT and IBM. Feynman's argument, later published as the paper Simulating Physics with Computers, was narrower and more precise than the sweeping claims that later grew up around it, and understanding what he actually proposed is a useful corrective to how the idea gets casually described today.

Feynman's observation was fundamentally about computational complexity. Simulating a quantum system of even a few dozen interacting particles on a classical computer requires tracking a number of variables that grows exponentially with the number of particles, because a full quantum state is described by amplitudes over every possible combination of the particles' individual states, not each particle separately. A system of only a few dozen quantum particles can require more numbers to describe its state fully than there are atoms in a computer's memory built to store them. Feynman's conclusion was blunt: nature itself is not classical, so if you want to simulate it efficiently, the simulator had better be quantum mechanical too.

This is important context for the broader theoretical promise of quantum computing that this guide discusses elsewhere: Feynman was not proposing a general-purpose faster computer for arbitrary tasks like sorting lists or running spreadsheets. He was proposing a special-purpose quantum simulator, a machine built from controllable quantum systems whose own quantum behavior would stand in for the quantum system a scientist wanted to study, in roughly the way a scale model in a wind tunnel stands in for the airflow around a real aircraft rather than calculating that airflow digitally.

The general-purpose quantum computer, the kind capable in principle of running Shor's or Grover's algorithm on arbitrary inputs, came later, built on separate theoretical work through the 1980s by researchers including David Deutsch, who formalized the idea of a universal quantum Turing machine in 1985. Feynman's talk supplied the founding intuition and the credibility of his name, but the leap from a quantum simulator beating a classical simulator at simulating quantum physics to a quantum computer beating a classical computer at factoring large numbers required substantial additional theoretical work, not an obvious or automatic extension.

This distinction matters for calibrating expectations today. Quantum simulation, in the narrow Feynman sense of using quantum hardware to model quantum chemistry or condensed matter physics, remains one of the more credible near-term applications discussed elsewhere in this guide, precisely because it is the use case the field's founding argument was actually about. Much of the broader excitement surrounding quantum computing, and much of the disappointment when that excitement does not materialize into results, comes from applications Feynman never claimed a quantum computer would solve in the first place.
